originalTitle: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
summary: Mark Zuckerberg's Meta made AI look so stinking cute by giving it a squishy little face - and this holiday season, he wants to sell you a Muse Charm so you can carry your jolly AI helper around like a Tamagotchi. But I won't be buying one, because we have Muse Charm at home. It […]
content: Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta made AI look so stinking cute by giving it a squishy little face — and this holiday season, he wants to sell you a Muse Charm so you can carry your jolly AI helper around like a Tamagotchi. But I won’t be buying one, because we have Muse Charm at home. It cost just $50, and I’ve decided the learning experience was worth it. [Media: https://www.tiktok.com/@verge/video/7702862550014168333] My version doesn’t sport cameras or a 5G cellular radio, but it really talks to Muse and has cute avatars, too! It doubles as a pocket watch and a remote camera viewfinder, and it can (theoretically) control my smart home. Or at least it can if you inject a lot of extra vibe code. Weeks ago, I paid $50 to get a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China — specifically the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C. Not only does the push-to-talk AI devkit look a lot like the Muse Charm, but it’s officially sanctioned by Meta. It’s one of the company’s first suggestions if you want to build a “Muse Gadget,” a device that uses Meta’s open-source code and tokens to directly connect to its Muse AI cloud. When the silver metal pocket watch arrived, it felt pretty useless to start. Setup was easy enough — I just plugged it into my PC and pointed Claude at Meta’s GitHub, then paired it to the Muse phone app. But even after I put Meta’s keys on the device, Muse originally thought I was sending it audio clips to transcribe rather than commands. After I cleared that up, Muse’s responses were still slow, and it didn’t answer me out loud. It was hard to tell what it was saying since it only showed a few words onscreen at a time, with no place to read full messages unless I whipped out my phone with its own Muse app. Meta’s build also only came with a single Jolly avatar that mostly just sat there and looked cute, and it wouldn’t automatically discover smart home gadgets like Amazon Echo or Google Home devices do. (This gadget really didn’t do anything useful after my initial install.) And though Meta AI software engineers Anant Narayanan and Jeremy Payne include a neat sample app showing how Muse Gadgets can stream video from your phone camera, the lack of a remote shutter button made it not so useful for taking photos. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/verge-sean-hollister-muse-gadget-331A2570-01-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] But a few sessions of Claude Code filled in almost all those holes. All I had to do was plug the Waveshare back into my PC, then ask Claude to reprogram each thing I wanted. When I complained to Claude that I couldn’t properly read or hear Muse’s replies to my asks, issues that others have mentioned as well, Claude built a conversation history page so I can swipe right to read what it said, and I plugged in a British AI voice from ElevenLabs that speaks its answers out loud. (The voice was the least soul-sucking of the ones in ElevenLabs’ free tier, my wife and I agree, even if it doesn’t match the Muse avatars’ cuddly vibe at all.) [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/verge-sean-hollister-muse-gadget-331A2576-01.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Thanks to Claude, I can now press a button to make my phone take a picture from across the room with a high-quality live preview, and my phone’s front-facing camera no longer displays upside down. Claude made fairly short work of adding a low-quality camera preview over Bluetooth, too, so I don’t need to be on home Wi-Fi to get photos from creative angles. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/DJI_20261030134230_0857_D-1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Muse_20261030_134155.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I asked Claude to make a whole batch of different avatars like the ones Meta showed off during Meta Connect, and to add a Tamagotchi-like minigame where they need food, play, sleep, and a bath. When the game seemed too simple to capture any attention, I had it add four different levels of hunger, boredom, and dirt. I decided treats should make a crunchy mess and get avatars dirtier when they eat them, and that too much play should tire out a pet. My wish was Claude’s command. When I noticed I was accidentally letting go of the push-to-talk button too soon and making Muse choke on almost-empty audio, vibe coding fixed it minutes later by sending only audio over one second in length. The only obvious lag I’m seeing now is from Meta’s own servers — sometimes they’re responsive, sometimes they lag quite a bit. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/verge-sean-hollister-muse-gadget-331A2577-01.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] It was so easy to let Claude reprogram the pendant that I asked it to build a few features specifically for this video in this story, including a working pocket watch face with three hands that actually tells the time. (That took it 15 minutes; now, when I say the hardware looks like a pocket watch, you can see what I mean!) It even found, downloaded, trimmed, and loaded video clips of Zuck introducing the Muse Charm and installed a video player so I could play those clips on the Waveshare. I want you to understand I have no coding experience, and so I have no idea if any of this code is good. It might be fatally flawed. Nor do I trust Meta or its Muse agent with my email or my home network, particularly after hearing how it leaked one reviewer’s home address. (I put it on guest Wi-Fi from the get-go as a precaution.) That means I don’t really know how useful a Muse Charm may or may not be for those who do know how to code and are willing to take a bigger leap of faith. But after nearly dropping a bulky little silver pendant a couple of times, one with no more Muse functionality than my phone (and quite a bit less without additional code), I’m thinking Muse itself isn’t the reason to buy a dedicated compute pocket watch. chineseContent: 马克·扎克伯格的 Meta 通过赋予 AI 一张柔软的小脸，让 AI 看起来非常可爱——而在这个假期，他想向你推销一个 Muse Charm，这样你就可以像电子蛋一样带着你快乐的 AI 助手到处走。但我不会买，因为我们家里有缪斯魅力。仅需 50 美元，我认为这次学习经历是值得的。 [媒体：https://www.tiktok.com/@verge/video/7702862550014168333]我的版本没有配备摄像头或5G蜂窝无线电，但它确实可以与Muse对话，并且还有可爱的头像！它兼作怀表和远程相机取景器，并且它可以（理论上）控制我的智能家居。或者至少如果您注入大量额外的氛围代码就可以。几周前，我花了 50 美元购买了从中国直运的 1.75 英寸触摸屏电脑挂件，特别是 Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C。一键通 AI 开发套件不仅看起来很像 Muse Charm，而且还得到了 Meta 的正式批准。如果你想构建一个“Muse Gadget”，这是该公司的首要建议之一，“Muse Gadget”是一种使用 Meta 的开源代码和代币直接连接到其 Muse AI 云的设备。当银色金属怀表到达时，感觉入手毫无用处。设置非常简单——我只需将它插入我的电脑，然后将 Claude 指向 Meta 的 GitHub，然后将其与 Muse 手机应用程序配对。但即使在我将 Meta 的按键放在设备上之后，Muse 最初也认为我是在向它发送音频剪辑来进行转录，而不是发送命令。当我弄清楚之后，Muse的反应仍然很慢，并没有大声回答我。很难说出它在说什么，因为它一次只在屏幕上显示几个单词，没有地方可以阅读完整的消息，除非我用自己的 Muse 应用程序拿出手机。 Meta 的构建也只配备了一个 Jolly 头像
